title: Share ration packs by household size
instruction: Each mat is a household, and the black pegs on the white card behind it show how many people live there. Share out all twelve ration packs so that every household gets the same number of packs per person.
context: Food-aid and food-bank distributions hand out rations per person, not per household: a family of three should receive three times what a person living alone receives. A robot that splits everything evenly treats households equally but not fairly; this task asks it to read each household's size and divide in proportion.
setup: World frame: x forward from the line through the two arm bases, y to the robot's left, measured from the midpoint between the bases; all on the bare table top. Mats (fixed, three identical blue-grey rubber mats, taped down): 200 x 200 x 5 mm, each spanning x 240-440 mm; left mat y 200-400 mm, middle mat y -100 to 100 mm, right mat y -400 to -200 mm (100 mm of bare table between neighbours). Cards (fixed, three white plastic or card strips, taped down): 40 x 200 x 6 mm, one directly behind each mat, x 445-485 mm, the same y span as its mat. Pegs (fixed, black wooden or plastic dowels glued upright to the cards): 20 mm across and 40 mm tall, centred at x = 465 mm and 50 mm apart; on the side cards they sit toward the table's midline: three behind the left mat (y = 210, 260, 310 mm), one behind the middle mat (y = 0), two behind the right mat (y = -285, -235 mm). Ration packs (loose, 12, all identical): orange cardboard cartons 70 mm long (along x), 55 mm wide (along y) and 35 mm tall, 150 g each (a boxed meal ration or a carton filled to that weight). They lie flat on the table in two rows across the front: row centres at x = 105 and 190 mm, columns at y = 360, 255, 150, -150, -255 and -360 mm (one pack at each of the twelve row-column crossings, long side along x).
scoring: A pack counts for a household when its centre (seen from above) is over that household's mat (the 200 x 200 mm square; not the card behind it) and its lowest point is at most 80 mm above the mat's top, in any orientation: flat, on its side, or stacked up to three high all count. Packs anywhere else (still at the front, on the table between mats, on a card, or still held) count for no household. Equity check first: the left household (3 people) must hold strictly more packs than the right household (2 people), which must hold strictly more than the middle household (1 person); if not (for example an even 4-4-4 split, swapped households, or everything on one mat), the score is 0. Otherwise each household earns 1/3 for exactly two packs per person (left 6, middle 2, right 4) and 1/6 for one pack more or one fewer than that; the score is the sum. So one pack left undistributed scores 5/6, and handing out one per person (3-1-2, six packs left over) scores 1/6. If any pack falls off the table (its centre below the table top) the score is 0. Full success (1.0): 6, 2 and 4 packs on the left, middle and right mats, all twelve at rest (under 1 cm/s) for 1 second. The score is taken at the end of the run.
reset_notes: Nothing is consumed. Put the twelve packs back in their two rows at the front; the mats, cards and pegs stay fixed to the table.
fidelity: Packs are rigid uniform boxes (no flexible carton, no contents shifting) with rubber-like friction (1.2 static, 1.0 dynamic), higher than bare cardboard. Each object carries one colour and there are no printed labels: household size is shown only by the number of pegs, which stand in for a printed household card or ration card. The mats, cards and pegs are rigid fixed boxes and cylinders. Gripper, arm and camera models are the station's own.
